extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science, journalists, policymakers, and readers interested in democracy and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of principles about how public opinion is formed and how leaders create, manage, and manipulate consent in democracies. Includes guidance on symbols, choice-presentation, morale, secrecy, propaganda technique, and the limits of direct democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate symbols to organize a following
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders must cultivate symbols which organize their following; symbols conserve unity by providing focal points where differences merge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples range from flags and totem poles to diluted ideological slogans. Symbols discharge emotion at a common target and blot out idiosyncratic ideas; leaders (even unbelievers) cherish them because they provide a handle to move a crowd. Anti-pattern: poking about with clear definitions and candid statements can break the transference of emotion and disintegrate unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present clear simplified choices for mass decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any mass decision requires necessary simplicity — voters typically can only say Yes or No (or rank choices in a preferential ballot); therefore leaders must present a concrete choice that connects to individual opinion through symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even complex matters must be reduced to an actionable choice for the Many. The effectiveness of mass action depends more on the quality of choices presented than on the number of ballots. Note that preferential ballots are more flexible but still depend on the choices provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small leadership bodies must formulate choices for the Many
rubrics_metrics.description: A small number of heads present a definite choice to a large group (e.g., caucus, nominating convention, steering committee); the Many can elect only after the Few have nominated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational mechanisms (caucus, convention, committees) exist because masses rarely formulate practical, detailed choices unaided. Anti-pattern: expecting spontaneous, fully-formed programs to arise synchronously across many minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct legislation and expanded balloting do not remove need for leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Initiative, referendum, and direct primary postpone or obscure the need for a machine; no amount of balloting obviates the need to create an issue on which voters can say Yes or No.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balloting compresses complex measures into abbreviated forms on a ballot — voters still decide in simplified terms. Thus 'direct legislation' is misleading: voting on an item is not the same as legislating its detailed content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must consider morale when planning policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders should evaluate decisions not only on merits but on their effect on the morale of those whose support is required; morale is good when individuals perform allotted parts with full energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In wartime this may mean limiting publication of casualties, spacing disclosure to avoid unified impressions, and otherwise managing information to prevent dissolution of units. Overexposure, candor, or large visible costs can provoke mutiny or collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer policies with remote or indirect incidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders favor programs whose costs or burdens are remote, postponed, or indirect because such costs are less likely to provoke immediate resistance from followers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aversion to direct taxation, preference for long-term debt, or policies where the foreigner is believed to pay. Local, visible costs (e.g., housing shortages) are harder to address because constructive solutions involve remote, complex factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control access to facts — leaders act as propagandists
rubrics_metrics.description: Established leaders typically have better information and control access to facts; every official functions to some degree as a censor and propagandist by selecting what the public is permitted to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders must choose which facts, in what setting and guise, to permit public knowledge — balancing institutional safety and candor. This selection shapes public understanding and consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use suggestion in news and publicity to shape mass responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is constantly exposed to suggestion: news is received with an aura indicating actions to be taken; reporters and stereotyped accounts predispose the mass to particular responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ostensible leader may be outmaneuvered by powerful newspaper proprietors or communicators. To shape consent, craft messages that emotionally and verbally connect new policies to preexisting vocalized feelings in the mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: In emergencies secure unity even without full consent
rubrics_metrics.description: When quick results are imperative, it is sometimes necessary to secure unity and flexibility without real consent; secrecy and centralization may be justified to avoid destructive public debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: military command decisions where public debate would dissolve armies. Trade-off: short-term mobility of the mass vs. long-term risks of dissimulation and loss of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek partial consent through trusted subordinates when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Wise leaders, when publicity won't unduly strengthen opposition or delay action, take subordinates sufficiently into confidence to prepare them so they feel they have freely willed the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This builds a measure of consent and reduces illusion in consultations; however, complexity means many will agree without full appreciation of contingencies — the practical limit of such consultation must be acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidate position by mending fences and limited concessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders maintain support by offering scapegoats, redressing minor grievances, rearranging jobs, placating factions, or performing small services for many people rather than attempting large, remote reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include favoring the influential or performing symbolic acts. The anonymous multitude is reached with propaganda rather than by individualized favors.

rubrics_metrics.name: The manufacture of consent now relies on analysis and technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasion has become a self-conscious art based on psychological research and modern means of communication; the creation of consent is now an analytic technic that alters political calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for practitioners: apply psychological insight and communications technology to craft persuasion. Implication for citizens: beware that traditional democratic assumptions about spontaneous, intuitive public opinion are undermined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizens should cultivate self-criticism and analyze opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: For democratic improvement, people must learn to use knowledge of how opinions are assembled to watch over their own opinions; realistic opinion requires time, study, measurement, and self-criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without ingrained habits of analyzing opinion when reading, talking, and deciding, the public is vulnerable to manipulation. Develop habits to detect 'buncombe' and prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume necessary political knowledge arises spontaneously
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratic dogma that the knowledge needed for management of human affairs comes spontaneously from the human heart is false; the outer world must be conceived and informed deliberately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus political intelligence must be cultivated; relying on intuition, conscience, or casual opinion is inadequate for complex policy-making.
